title: Act V, Scene I
focus: the guilt that will not wash away

teacherSummary.text: A Doctor and a Gentlewoman watch Lady Macbeth sleepwalk with a taper; she has light by her continually, by her own command. She rubs her hands as if washing them ('Out, damned spot!'), recalls the murder of Duncan ('who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him?'), Lady Macduff ('The Thane of Fife had a wife: where is she now?') and Banquo, and says 'What's done cannot be undone.' The Doctor says she needs 'the divine' more than the physician.

context.history: Lady Macbeth speaks in prose here, though earlier she spoke commanding verse; prose often marks madness or loss of control in Shakespeare.

significance: The scene reverses II.ii: water no longer clears her, darkness frightens her, and her buried guilt surfaces. Her lines replay the play's crimes in fragments.
discussionQuestions: Can people truly escape guilt by refusing to think about it?
Where does imagery appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with fate and free will?

satQuestions.passage:
What is it she does now? Look, how she rubs her hands.
It is an accustomed action with her, to seem thus washing her hands: I have known her continue in this a quarter of an hour.
Yet here’s a spot.
Hark! she speaks: I will set down what comes from her, to satisfy my remembrance the more strongly.
Out, damned spot! out, I say!—One: two: why, then, ’tis time to do’t.—Hell is murky!—Fie, my lord, fie! a soldier, and afeard? What need we fear who knows it, when none can call our power to account?—Yet who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him.
Do you mark that?
The thane of Fife had a wife: where is she now?—What, will these hands ne’er be clean?—No more o’ that, my lord, no more o’ that: you mar all with this starting.
Go to, go to; you have known what you should not.
She has spoke what she should not, I am sure of that: heaven knows what she has known.
Here’s the smell of the blood still: all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand. Oh, oh, oh!

segments.script: Lady Macbeth speaks in prose here, though earlier she spoke commanding verse; prose often marks madness or loss of control in Shakespeare. The scene reverses II.ii: water no longer clears her, darkness frightens her, and her buried guilt surfaces. Her lines replay the play's crimes in fragments. Characterization: Lady Macbeth sleepwalks, washing her hands, reliving the murders in prose. Structure: She speaks prose; her verse control is gone. Imagery: Blood, the smell of blood, "all the perfumes of Arabia." Watch for the prophecies: The Witches' riddling prophecies: notice how each promise shapes what Macbeth hopes, fears and does next.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Out, damned spot! out, I say” slowly and put it in my own words: Sleepwalking, Lady Macbeth tries to rub away an imaginary spot of blood from her hand. Next, craft. I notice the frantic commands, "Out, damned spot! out, I say," spoken to something that is not there. The strongest word is “spot”: the tiny stain stands for guilt she cannot wash away. Then, effect. What does Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking show about her? My answer: Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking shows that she is broken by guilt; the woman who said "a little water clears us of this deed" now reveals in her sleep what her waking self hid.

segments.script: Annotate the scene for characterization, structure (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about the guilt that will not wash away? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act V, Scene I develops the idea of the guilt that will not wash away. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) When the text says “Here’s the smell of the blood still: all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand” (Act V, Scene I, line 2036), it shows this directly. She once said "A little water clears us of this deed," but now cries "all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand."

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
